newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan banks call for right to sell mutual funds.
newsitem.headline: Japan banks call for right to sell mutual funds.

text.p: Japanese banks are asking regulators to open the door for them to tap directly into Japan's huge business of selling and managing mutual funds.

Banks are keen to use their extensive branch networks to directly sell mutual funds, called investment trust funds in Japan, to depositors throughout the country and to diversify the range of businesses they offer.
Although banks have investment trust affiliates these have few branches, and banks themselves are not allowed to sell or manage such funds.
Rather than managing the funds, the banks are eager to sell the variety of investment trust funds available to individuals in order to earn commissions.

"In the United States, outstanding mutual funds total nearly 200 trillion yen ($1.829 trillion). But in Japan, they are only about 50 trillion yen ($457.46 billion)," said an offical at a major commercial bank.
"The figures show Japan's investment trust market has the potential to grow much bigger," he said.
The popular perception in Japan is that ordinary individual investors show little interest in trusts as they are poorly run.
However, the bank official said the slowness in sales of investment trusts was due to insufficient sales efforts by brokerages.
Poor returns on stock investments have also kept small investors away from the funds, industry sources said.

"I don't think major Japanese brokers are serious about selling investment trusts offered by bank affiliates," the bank official said. "We think we are quite good at managing the trusts, so we need the effective sales channel."
Banking sources said the banks' long-established credibility could help polish the image of investment trusts.
Most of Japan's investment trusts are managed by brokerages' subsidiaries and sold via stock sales staff at brokerages.
To boost competition and attractiveness of the trusts, the Finance Ministry allowed banks to join the investment trust management business through their affiliates in 1993.

The ministry also took steps in late 1994 to improve the performance of the investment trusts and increase their transparency to attract more small investors. But data from the Investment Trusts Association show net assets of stock investment trusts have continued to fall since the early 1990s.

Net assets of stock investment trusts totalled 13.53 trillion yen ($123.79 billion) at the end of July, down from 45.55 trillion yen ($416.74 billion) at their peak at the end of 1989, when Tokyo's Nikkei stock average hit a record 38,957.44. On Wednesday, the Nikkei closed at 21,156.75.

Takashi Tamaki, chairman of the Regional Banks Association of Japan, has said the industry group would ask the government to implement deregulation, including of sales of investment trusts at bank branches. His remarks follow similar requests which Japan's 10 biggest banks made to the government in August.
The Securities and Exchange Council, an advisory body to the finance minister, is expected to examine the issue soon.
However, brokerages are not happy about the idea of banks crossing into their traditional territory.
"If such sales are allowed by banks, they will only sell investment trusts offered by their affiliates," said an executive at Nomura Securities.
An official at another brokerage said: "I doubt bank officials will be able to deal with the situation when the value of a trust fall below face value." ($1=109.30 yen)
